HONG KONG, China (CNN) -- From the runway to the store rack, Vivienne Tam is one designer who uses creativity and business acumen in equal measure. Leading fashion designer Vivienne Tam spoke to CNN's Andrew Stevens in The Boardroom. Since her start in the fashion business in the early '80s and establishing her own brand in the '90s, she has risen to fame with her east-meets-west styles. Today it's her skills in business which have expanded the label to some 30 stores worldwide, from New York to Beijing. CNN's Andrew Stevens caught up with the designer in Hong Kong to talk about what it's like to lead both the business and creative direction of a global fashion line. Tam: The business side is like designing, it's like I like the touch of the fabric, I like to know the details about it. And you feel about it, you know about the deal, because who's the person who knows what the best deal for you is? Yourself. It's like designing clothes, I love to know how to solve every single thing, you know. Like what kind of budget . Stevens: It's just natural curiosity? Tam: Natural curiosity, I love it. I love every aspect of it. Stevens: Who have you learned your business skills from or have you made it up as you went along? Tam: I self-taught myself in business; I know nothing about the business, I learned everything -- about the pricing, the shipping, the contracts, everything -- by doing it. When you're doing it yourself, you know everything. If you don't do it, you just listen to somebody telling you how to do it, you're not experiencing it. Once you're experiencing it, you can grow so much from it. Once you experience it, you can go further, much further. It's a feeling of it. Stevens: When you won the Hong Kong businesswoman of the year award, you said that your mother was one of your greatest inspirations. How did she inspire you? Tam: She inspired me so much you know, like you say, the determination, persistence. When she really wanted to make something, she would really go to the end, she'd really want to make it happen and I see her, she's really the force behind me. We were quite poor, we had no money, my parents were working really hard. When I grew up, I saw them working so hard, and then deep inside myself that I wanted to change the situation, I wanted to make something, this one thing. Stevens: What do you think are the most important qualities for a businessperson? Tam: For me, it's most important, a vision, determination, and to never say no to yourself. And be open to criticisms, open to learning, and open to criticisms and knowing nothing about the business; nothing, so you can learn everything by knowing nothing, you know, and be successful in the things that you didn't know. Stevens: You work in a very creative industry, how do you keep your staff motivated in this industry, how do you keep them going, how do you keep them working for you? Tam: I always tell them my story, how I was in school when my teacher asked for one outfit -- I give them 8 outfits. I told them, do things that I didn't ask you, give me, do your work with passion, it's more important than "Oh, 6 o'clock, I have to leave." Do something that is out of the box. E-mail to a friend .

**HONG KONG, China (CNN) —** From the runway to the store rack, Vivienne Tam is a designer who combines creativity and business acumen in equal measure.

Leading fashion designer Vivienne Tam spoke with CNN’s Andrew Stevens in *The Boardroom*. Since entering the fashion business in the early 1980s and establishing her own brand in the 1990s, she has risen to prominence with her East-meets-West designs. Today, her business skills have helped expand the label to some 30 stores worldwide, from New York to Beijing.

CNN’s Andrew Stevens caught up with the designer in Hong Kong to discuss what it is like to oversee both the business and creative direction of a global fashion line.

**Tam:** The business side is like designing. Just as I like the feel of the fabric, I also like to understand every detail. You develop a feel for the business and learn about the deal, because who knows what the best deal is for you? You do. It’s like designing clothes: I love knowing how to solve every single issue, such as determining the right budget.

**Stevens:** Is it simply natural curiosity?

**Tam:** Natural curiosity. I love it. I love every aspect of it.

**Stevens:** From whom did you learn your business skills, or did you make things up as you went along?

**Tam:** I taught myself about business. I knew nothing about it, so I learned everything—pricing, shipping, contracts, everything—by doing it. When you do things yourself, you understand every aspect. If you don’t do it and merely listen to someone telling you how, you aren’t truly experiencing it. Once you experience it, you can grow so much. You can go further—much further. You develop a feel for it.

**Stevens:** When you won the Hong Kong Businesswoman of the Year award, you said that your mother was one of your greatest inspirations. How did she inspire you?

**Tam:** She inspired me so much through her determination and persistence. When she truly wanted to accomplish something, she would see it through to the end. She was determined to make it happen. I saw that in her, and she has truly been the force behind me.

We were quite poor and had no money. My parents worked very hard. Growing up, I watched them work so hard, and deep inside, I knew that I wanted to change our situation. I wanted to create something and achieve this one goal.

**Stevens:** What do you think are the most important qualities for a businessperson?

**Tam:** For me, the most important qualities are vision, determination, and never saying no to yourself. You must also be open to criticism and learning. Even if you know nothing about business—nothing—you can learn everything by starting from that position, and you can succeed in areas you previously knew nothing about.

**Stevens:** You work in a highly creative industry. How do you keep your staff motivated? How do you keep them going and working for you?

**Tam:** I always tell them my story. When I was in school and my teacher asked for one outfit, I gave her eight. I tell my staff: do things I haven’t asked you to do. Approach your work with passion. That is more important than thinking, “Oh, it’s six o’clock; I have to leave.” Do something outside the box.

outputs.L2:
**HONG KONG, China (CNN)** — Vivienne Tam combines artistic talent with commercial expertise, guiding her designs from the catwalk to retail stores.

The prominent fashion designer joined CNN’s Andrew Stevens in *The Boardroom*. After entering the fashion industry in the early 1980s and launching her own label in the 1990s, Tam became renowned for designs that blend Eastern and Western influences. Her business abilities have since helped grow the brand to roughly 30 stores around the world, including locations in New York and Beijing.

Stevens met Tam in Hong Kong to discuss how she manages both the commercial operations and the creative vision of an international fashion brand.

**Tam:** To me, managing a business is similar to creating a design. Just as I want to feel a fabric and understand every detail about it, I also want to understand every element of a business agreement. After all, no one knows what arrangement is best for you better than you do. As with making clothes, I enjoy finding solutions to every issue, including questions about budgets.

**Stevens:** So it comes from an instinctive desire to learn?

**Tam:** Yes, it is natural curiosity, and I enjoy it. I’m interested in every part of the process.

**Stevens:** Did someone teach you how to run a business, or did you learn along the way?

**Tam:** I taught myself. At the beginning, I knew absolutely nothing about business. I learned about prices, deliveries, contracts, and everything else through direct experience. When you handle matters personally, you gain a complete understanding. Simply hearing someone explain how something should be done is not the same as going through it yourself. Firsthand experience helps you develop and enables you to progress much further. You begin to acquire an instinct for it.

**Stevens:** When you received Hong Kong’s Businesswoman of the Year award, you identified your mother as one of your biggest influences. In what way did she inspire you?

**Tam:** She had an enormous impact on me, particularly through her perseverance and determination. Whenever she decided to accomplish something, she followed it through completely and did everything possible to make it happen. I regard her as the driving force behind me. My family was quite poor and had very little money, so both of my parents worked extremely hard. Watching them struggle while I was growing up created a deep desire in me to improve our circumstances and achieve something meaningful.

**Stevens:** Which characteristics do you consider essential for someone in business?

**Tam:** In my view, the key qualities are vision, determination, and refusing to tell yourself that something cannot be done. You must also welcome criticism and remain willing to learn. Beginning with no business knowledge can actually allow you to absorb everything. That openness can help you succeed in areas that were once unfamiliar to you.

**Stevens:** Fashion is an especially creative field. How do you encourage your employees, sustain their enthusiasm, and persuade them to continue working with you?

**Tam:** I often share a story from my school days. When a teacher requested one outfit, I produced eight. I encourage my staff to go beyond what I specifically ask of them and to approach their responsibilities with passion. That matters more than simply watching the clock and leaving at 6 p.m. I want them to think unconventionally and contribute more than expected.

*Send this article to a friend.*

Vivienne Tam built a globally recognized fashion brand by combining her creative talent with strong business acumen. Her signature east-meets-west aesthetic brought together cultural influences in a distinctive and contemporary way, helping her rise to international prominence and expand her label to approximately 30 stores worldwide.

For Tam, business is not separate from the creative process but an extension of design itself. She approaches both with curiosity, close attention to detail, and a willingness to solve problems directly. As her company grew, she taught herself the practical skills needed to manage it, including pricing, shipping, contract negotiation, and budgeting. Much of this knowledge came through hands-on experience and learning from the challenges she encountered along the way.

Tam also credits her mother as one of her greatest sources of inspiration. Her mother’s determination, persistence, and resilience shaped Tam’s outlook and encouraged her to keep moving forward despite obstacles. Together, these qualities—creativity, discipline, curiosity, and perseverance—have played a central role in Tam’s success as both a designer and an entrepreneur.

CNN’s Andrew Stevens interviewed fashion designer Vivienne Tam about the challenges of combining creative leadership with the practical demands of running an international business. Best known for blending Eastern and Western influences, Tam has built a distinctive fashion label that reflects both her Chinese heritage and her experience in the global marketplace. Her role extends far beyond designing collections: she also remains closely involved in the commercial decisions needed to turn creative ideas into a sustainable brand.

Tam explained that she learned many aspects of business through direct experience rather than formal training. As her company developed, she taught herself how to price garments, manage shipping, negotiate contracts, and prepare budgets. Understanding these details allowed her to make informed decisions and maintain control over the direction of the label. Although the process was demanding, it gave her a practical grasp of how each part of the company contributes to its overall success.

Her persistence was shaped in part by her mother, whose determination provided an important example. That influence encouraged Tam to keep moving forward despite the obstacles involved in building a fashion business from the ground up. Instead of separating creativity from management, she treated both as essential parts of entrepreneurship.

This combination of artistic vision, business discipline, and perseverance helped Tam expand her East-meets-West brand to roughly 30 stores worldwide. Her experience shows that success in fashion depends on more than talent alone. It also requires a willingness to learn, close attention to operational details, and the resilience to continue through setbacks. By remaining both the creative force behind the label and an active participant in its daily management, Tam demonstrated the value of hands-on leadership and sustained determination.

**Hong Kong, China**

Hong Kong is a vibrant city and Special Administrative Region of China, located on the country’s southern coast. Known for its dramatic skyline, natural harbor, and fast-paced economy, Hong Kong has long served as an important gateway between China and the rest of the world.

The city combines Chinese traditions with international influences. Visitors can explore historic temples, lively street markets, modern shopping districts, hiking trails, and famous attractions such as Victoria Peak and Victoria Harbour. Cantonese is widely spoken, while Chinese and English are official languages.

Hong Kong became a British colony in the nineteenth century and returned to Chinese sovereignty in 1997. Today, it operates under the “one country, two systems” framework. With its distinctive history, culture, and economic role, Hong Kong remains one of China’s most internationally recognized cities.
